items.title: Bowman, The U.S. Economy and Considerations for Monetary Policy
items.excerpt: Speech At the C. Peter McColough Series on International Economics Council on Foreign Relations, Washington, D.C.
body: Good afternoon. It is a pleasure to join you today at the Council on Foreign Relations to discuss my outlook for the U.S. economy.1

Economic growth has gained momentum this year, driven by robust investment demand and solid consumer spending, and the labor market now appears to have stabilized. These outcomes suggest that the policy rate cuts toward the end of last year helped to address some labor market weakness. We are experiencing rapid technological change and ongoing geopolitical tensions, while inflation pressures have persisted for longer than I had hoped and have shown recent signs of broadening. Despite these challenges, increased investment in and use of artificial intelligence (AI), or super intelligence, are boosting economic growth and productivity and American families appear to be resilient.

The Federal Reserve's monetary policy goals are to achieve maximum employment and price stability. While the labor market has improved more than I expected this year, our progress on lowering inflation has disappointed. Therefore, bringing inflation down remains a priority. I am also monitoring expectations about AI and energy prices, and how they influence the risks to achieving our mandates. Consistent with my views following our September FOMC meeting, I continue to focus on interpreting the underlying trends in the economy and the evolution of financial conditions.2

In my remarks today, I will review our most recent FOMC policy meeting and discuss current economic conditions and my near-term outlook for the economy. I will then turn to recent developments in energy markets and the AI buildout and will conclude with my thoughts on the appropriate path of monetary policy.

Update on the Most Recent FOMC Meeting At last month's FOMC meeting, I joined my colleagues to support holding the federal funds rate target range at 3-3/4 to 4 percent. This approach was consistent with my view that further changes in the policy rate should wait until we had a better understanding of how conditions would evolve and how the recent rate increase would influence the underlying trends in the economy. Maintaining the policy stance at the October meeting allowed us to assess the incoming data. While I continue to expect that several of the factors currently boosting inflation will abate next year, currently inflation has proven to be more persistent than I had anticipated. It is also important to gain greater clarity on the effect of recent market volatility on financial conditions.

Economic and Financial Conditions U.S. economic growth has stepped up this year. After rising a solid 2.4 percent during the first half of the year, real gross domestic product (GDP) likely increased at an even stronger pace of more than 3 percent in the third quarter, well above last year's 2 percent pace.3 Economic growth has been supported by robust increases in AI-related capital expenditures and solid consumer spending. However, some interest-rate-sensitive sectors like residential investment have declined, and the recent rise in mortgage rates appears to be dragging home construction and sales down further. Consumer spending has strengthened this year, despite softness in real incomes and declining sentiment, which are partly due to higher energy prices.

Labor Market Conditions Labor market conditions look to have improved since last year. Over the course of this year, the unemployment rate has edged down to 4.1 percent in October, remaining close to my estimate of its natural rate. Job gains have been above last year's anemic pace, averaging about 80,000 per month through October, and have broadened across industries beyond health care and social assistance.

The labor market continues to show low dynamism, with low-hiring and low-firing conditions as we sometimes see in a late-cycle expansion. The job-finding rate has been low, especially for new labor force entrants, and the share of long-term unemployed workers has moved up significantly. Workers' perceptions of job availability in the Conference Board survey have remained soft in recent months. On their own, these data would be consistent with a higher unemployment rate than currently reported. However, layoffs have moved down this year, offsetting the softness in hiring. In plain terms, workers are both less likely to find a new job and less likely to be laid off, a somewhat unusual pattern.

Although stable, the labor market does not appear to be tight, as wage growth has slowed to a modest pace. On a 12-month basis, the wages and salaries component of the employment cost index increased 3.1 percent in September, the same pace as the change in average hourly earnings for October. Both measures have slowed noticeably from a year ago. An increasing number of workers have taken on a supplemental part-time job to make ends meet, as the share of multiple job holders has increased back to levels seen in early 2025. Given strong productivity gains in recent years, wage growth at this pace is in line with or even below the pace we would expect if inflation was running at 2 percent.

Inflation Progress on lowering inflation has stalled over the past two years or so. Today's consumer price index suggests that 12-month core PCE inflation likely moved up further to 3.3 percent in October, as upward pressures from higher energy prices and AI-related demand continue to flow through to core goods and services prices.

Lack of progress on lowering inflation largely reflects a confluence of shocks unrelated to conditions in the labor market. Tariffs, energy, and AI-related price pressures each accounted for roughly one-fourth of above-target core PCE inflation over the 12 months ending in September. The remaining one-fourth likely reflects persistent effects from the inflationary shocks in recent years. Price pressures had been concentrated in a few categories, but the latest data suggest that these pressures may be broadening.

It is important to ensure that those inflationary pressures do not intensify, further broaden, or become embedded in consumer and business expectations. But today's consumer price index data suggest that inflation pressures may persist for longer. Tariff effects should further wane going forward. Energy-related price pressures should unwind when the Middle East conflict resolves. And inflation pressures related to the AI buildout seem to persist despite some early signs of slowing. I mostly view these pressures as reflecting relative price shocks in specific sectors of the economy. For example, the AI buildout has quickly shifted investment demand toward specific types of high-tech capital, putting upward pressure on prices due to relatively inelastic supply in the near term. As these shocks wane or unwind and with no inflationary pressures emerging in the labor market, my forecast is for core PCE inflation to move closer to 2 percent next year.

Financial Conditions Financial conditions have tightened a bit recently because of lower equity prices, higher private interest rates, and a stronger dollar. That tightening comes against a backdrop of increased market volatility. Corporate bond and mortgage rate spreads have widened, and equity valuations in the tech sector have dropped, as investors appear to be reassessing expected returns and the risks associated with increased external financing for AI investment projects.

Economic Outlook and Risks Looking ahead, my expectation is that policies designed to boost the economic potential of the U.S. economy would continue to support productivity, growth, and business confidence. These policies include pragmatic regulations, lower taxes, and more supportive policies toward businesses. I expect the labor market to remain stable and inflation to slow, as special factors currently holding inflation elevated gradually wane or unwind next year. Over time, I also expect increased AI adoption to raise productivity and put some downward pressure on inflation as lower production costs are passed through to consumer prices.

On risks to the outlook, with the labor market improving since last year, I am more attentive to the inflation side of our mandate. Sustained supply-chain pressures from the AI buildout or greater pass-through of higher energy costs could cause inflation pressures to persist. I can also envision a scenario in which the effects of the Middle East conflict and the tech investment boom wane or unwind quickly. In this scenario, I would also expect a timelier return of core PCE inflation toward our target.

I also see a number of risks to the outlook for economic activity, many originating in financial markets. These risks include a large correction in equity valuations, if returns on AI investment fall short of expectations, and a sharp increase in private longer-term interest rates. Lower equity prices could undermine the resilience in consumer spending. And higher interest rates could further strain interest-rate-sensitive sectors of the economy, like housing and small business investment. I will continue to closely monitor developments in credit and equity markets to assess risks to economic growth and financial stability.

Important Issues for Monetary Policy I see conditions in energy markets and the AI buildout as two important issues for the economy in the months ahead. Developments in these two areas could have material effects on both sides of our mandate and could influence my views on the path for monetary policy.

Energy Markets The Middle East conflict has disrupted energy markets, impairing the flow of oil and other commodities passing through the Strait of Hormuz, which accounted for about 20 percent of global oil supply before the conflict-roughly equivalent to total U.S. oil consumption. As tensions rose, Brent oil prices moved up to and above $110 per barrel in the second half of October before dropping sharply last week on optimism that an agreement between the U.S. and Iran could be reached following the midterm elections. Although crude oil flows in the Persian Gulf have recovered to near pre-conflict levels in recent weeks, freight rates and insurance premiums have surged because of more complex logistics and ongoing geopolitical risk, raising the cost of delivered oil to many markets around the world.

Prices for gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel also moved up to near or even above their highs in the spring. These higher prices reflected both higher crude oil prices and wider refining margins, as refineries in both the Persian Gulf and Russia have been damaged as a result of ongoing military conflicts in both regions. Prices for refined products have retraced some of the earlier gains more recently as crude oil prices have receded and margins have shown signs of normalizing.

While the outcomes of these conflicts remain uncertain, my approach is to look through temporary energy-driven inflation, when possible, and to remain alert to signs that it is spreading into broader prices or expectations. If geopolitical tensions persist, energy prices may stay elevated in the near term, increasing risks that core inflation may also stay elevated because of increased pass-through to consumer prices of higher production and transportation costs.

Although the U.S. economy is now a net exporter of oil products and less energy intensive, we could still see an impact on economic activity from higher energy prices. The recent deterioration in consumer sentiment measures suggests households may be internalizing a more persistent reduction in their purchasing power. I would be especially concerned about effects on both sides of our mandate if there were further significant disruptions to energy markets. An escalation of geopolitical tensions could have more meaningful effects on real activity because of higher uncertainty and the larger impact of energy prices on lower- and middle-income consumers.

Even with a quick resolution to the Middle East conflict, it may take some time for energy prices to normalize. Futures markets expect oil prices to decline only gradually, as global oil consumption is projected to exceed supply at least through the end of this year. As inventories have been drawn down, the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) has reached a bit less than 50 days of crude oil imports, the lowest level since the early 1980s, reflecting both this year's and the larger 2022 SPR releases. A number of new Gulf pipelines to bypass the Strait of Hormuz are under construction or expansion, with the United Arab Emirates' West-East expansion coming online in early 2027 and most others in 2028 and beyond. Domestic oil production could also continue to rise, which would put downward pressure on fuel costs.

AI Buildout In remarks earlier this year, I discussed the responsible use of AI in the financial system.4 Today I will describe how this technology is shaping the broader economy. Given the transformative promise of this technology, investment in data centers has boomed and has been a major influence on the U.S. economy. With plans for new data centers continuing to surge, I expect the AI shock to play out over some time. However, as these investments are increasingly being financed with external funds, including off-balance-sheet liabilities, I am also focused on potential risks to the economy and financial stability if revenues from AI customers disappoint.

We may still be in the early days when investment rises rapidly while workers and firms determine the best use cases before we see more meaningful effects on productivity. The boom in data center investment is undeniable, with growth in real business fixed investment strengthening further this year to a pace like the 1990s tech boom. High-tech equipment, software, and data center construction have accounted for the large majority of growth in business investment since 2025, with gains broadening to other categories this year.

AI adoption has grown significantly, especially among larger firms, with about 25 percent of businesses and roughly 10 percent of workers reporting using AI every day in their work. However, use varies greatly across industries and occupations, with stronger adoption in information and other business services sectors. I think there is a risk that some workers will be displaced as firms adopt this technology, even as others see their productivity-and wages-rise. Monetary policy cannot address that transition directly, but it should support a dynamic labor market that facilitates the necessary retraining and mobility of workers across jobs.

AI revenues have been rising quickly but are not yet sufficient to pay for the expense of maintaining existing and developing new AI models and data centers. As capital spending has surged, hyperscalers and other companies have increasingly been sourcing funds from credit and equity markets. And as investors see an increased risk in these investments, the cost of financing has been rising notably.

In addition to financing costs, the AI buildout is also putting upward pressure on a number of price categories. Prices of memory chips, semiconductors, computers, and other electronic products have increased sharply this year-in a few categories by double digits-as demand from data centers has outpaced supply. I expect production capacity to catch up to demand gradually over time.

AI-related debt has been rising rapidly, with notable gains in corporate bonds, private credit, and project finance, and is on track to exceed $800 billion this year. Other obligations, in the form of long-term lease and contract commitments and residual value guarantees, have also surged and their potential payments are estimated at more than three times the amount of debt. Given their strong credit ratings, hyperscalers and large tech firms have assumed off-balance-sheet liabilities to allow smaller and riskier companies to use them as collateral in asset-based financing for data center construction and the purchase of accelerated computing equipment. These connections among AI firms have also been accompanied by hyperscalers and chip designers making equity investments in smaller companies that purchase their products, creating the appearance of circular financing.

The largest U.S. bank holding companies have some exposure to AI-related financing, which is scrutinized during annual supervisory stress tests. Life insurance companies, pension funds, private credit, and mutual funds also have exposure. Most of these entities are well capitalized and have stable funding. But the complex nature of the financing structures makes it difficult to properly assess counterparty risk.

Risks seem to be concentrated in only a few large firms that provide AI services, including AI labs and the hyperscalers. If AI-related revenues fall short of sharply rising costs, especially as public sentiment and local opposition could lead to increased regulation and delays, we could see a sharp correction in equity prices for AI firms, higher financing costs, and reduced access to credit. This shock would likely slow the AI buildout and soften both economic activity and inflation.

We may have already seen some reassessment of expected returns play out in recent weeks as equity valuations dropped, corporate bond spreads widened, and credit default swaps increased for some companies involved in the AI buildout. I will be looking at how momentum in adoption of and investment in this technology evolves and for possible effects on both inflation and employment.

The Path Forward for Monetary Policy As we think about the path ahead, it is important to remember that over the past two years the U.S. economy has experienced successive inflationary shocks that have not been driven by labor market conditions. Monetary policy cannot offset the direct effects of tariffs and energy costs on inflation, but it plays a central role in containing the second-round effects. Monetary policy also has limited influence on AI-related price pressures. However, in certain segments of AI-intensive sectors, particularly among newer and medium-sized firms, higher interest rates appear to be holding back investment and purchasing decisions.

As I noted earlier, financial conditions have tightened. Against this backdrop, the benefit of additional policy tightening has to be carefully weighed against its costs for interest-rate-sensitive sectors. The October Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey on Bank Lending Practices (SLOOS) suggests that the concentration of demand weakness in real estate loan categories reflects existing headwinds in those sectors.5

Time will help us learn more about the durability of momentum in AI-related demand and the evolution of geopolitical risks, both of which could be critical in the months ahead for setting our policy stance. Greater clarity on AI-related financing conditions and the sustainability of AI investments should increase my confidence in future policy decisions. Geopolitical conditions affect commodity markets and the degree of economic uncertainty perceived by households and businesses.

Before our next meeting in December, we will receive the PCE inflation report for October and the employment report for November. Today, I am seeing signs that inflation pressures are persisting, while labor market conditions appear to be firming. This indicates that there is still work to do to bring inflation closer to 2 percent. Given the recent market volatility, I will also continue to closely monitor how developments in financial conditions influence the economic outlook.

In the meantime, I will continue to meet with a broad range of contacts to inform my assessment of economic conditions and the appropriate stance of policy. It is important to remember that monetary policy is not on a preset course. At each FOMC meeting, my colleagues and I will evaluate incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the implications for the risks to our dual-mandate goals of maximum employment and price stability.
Thank you again for the invitation to join you this afternoon. I look forward to our discussion.
1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) or the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System.
2. See Atlantic Council (2026), "Federal Reserve Vice Chair Michelle Bowman on Modernizing Financial Regulation," AC Front Page event, Washington, October 1.

3. Note that currently reported GDP growth in the first half of this year may be overestimated by about 0.3 percentage point, reflecting downward revisions in the retail sales annual update that were not folded into the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) 2026 annual revision of the national accounts.

4. See Michelle W. Bowman (2026), "Artificial Intelligence in the Financial System," (PDF) remarks delivered at the Financial Stability Oversight Council Artificial Intelligence Series Roundtable on Cybersecurity and Risk Management, Washington, May 1.
5. The October 2026 SLOOS is available on the Board's website at https://www.federalreserve.gov/data/sloos/sloos-202610.htm.

Waller, The Economic Outlook and Some Thoughts on Labor Market Dynamism
items.excerpt: Speech At the Bank of England Watchers Conference King’s Business School and Money, Macro and Finance Society, London, United Kingdom
body: Thank you, Paul, and welcome to Bank of England watchers, who I suspect are watching the Federal Reserve as well.1

My subject today is the outlook for the U.S. economy and the implications for monetary policy. I think there is little disagreement about the basics of that outlook. The U.S. economy is growing strongly, with a labor market that has brought employment close to its long-term rate. But inflation remains too high, so I will explain why I believe further tightening of monetary policy will be needed, sooner rather than later, to return inflation to a path that will reach 2 percent in the medium term.

The outline of my speech is to first explain why I voted to hold the policy rate steady at the most recent meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). Then I will talk about the general state of the U.S. economy. After that, I will ask some open-ended questions about the dynamism of the U.S. labor market that are important to consider over the longer run. I'll follow that by a discussion of recent inflation data and then describe my views about the future path of monetary policy.

At our most recent meeting, I supported the FOMC majority in holding monetary policy at its current setting. As I said in a speech a couple weeks before then, my rationale was that the Committee's communication about the likely tightening of policy had already led financial markets to price in some tightening.2 When this communication is clear and credible, what really matters is that those hikes are eventually carried out-it is not necessary, for example, to raise rates at consecutive meetings.

If, however, the hikes are not carried out, markets will reduce expectations of rate hikes and rates will immediately fall, which would loosen monetary policy in an undesirable way. So, while the precise timing of the hikes doesn't matter, ensuring that the promised hikes are implemented in a reasonable period of time does.

Let me turn to the economy. Economic output continues to grow at a healthy pace. The initial estimate was that real gross domestic product (GDP) rose 3.4 percent in the third quarter, supported by strong consumer spending and robust investment. Consumption growth was helped by a booming stock market, and investment by businesses continued to surge, especially in high-tech equipment associated with the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout. I expect GDP growth is backing off a bit in the current quarter, as consumer spending slows to levels that I think are more consistent with household income and wealth, but output will continue to grow at a solid pace.

The labor market has also been solid. The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1 percent in October, the same rate it was over the summer. Job creation, which has been fluctuating widely month to month for some time, saw October gains of 165,000 jobs and 85,000 jobs added to estimates of the previous two months. To look through the volatility, the 6-month and 12-month average payroll gains have been closer to 80,000 jobs a month. This level is a bit above most estimates of the breakeven level needed to keep the unemployment rate steady but entirely consistent with my view that the supply and demand for labor are in rough balance.

While the labor market has been stable, for over a year now it has been what is best characterized as "low hire, low fire." One can understand this characterization by looking at job separation and hiring rates today and comparing them with what they were before the pandemic (see figures 1 and 2). You will see that the rate of separations, the sum of layoffs and quits, has been persistently low the past few years compared with a decade ago. The hiring rate is also low. This is unusual because, in a strong labor market, the hiring rate is usually high. Hiring tends to be low when the labor market is weak, which is when the firing rate is often elevated. What is unusual today, and may be unprecedented, is the extent to which both firing and hiring are now so low.

These data have led me to consider a question that has longer-term implications for the economy and monetary policy: Does a stable labor market necessarily mean it's a healthy labor market? To illustrate the difference, if your mom was in the hospital and the doctor told you her condition was stable, you would be relieved but you wouldn't say she is healthy. I am concerned that the low hire, low fire equilibrium in the labor market means it has lost some of its dynamism, which is important for productivity growth and real wages. If the labor market is in fact showing less dynamism, is it an issue for monetary policy? While I don't have answers to these questions, I do think the questions are worth asking.

This discussion starts with distinguishing between net employment growth and gross flows in and out of employment. Behind the monthly job creation numbers that get most of the world's attention is the enormous churn in the labor market. For example, the 60,000 jobs created in September was a net change in the level of employment, but it is dwarfed by the more than 5 million people who left their jobs that month and the more than 5 million who were hired. Despite the low separation and hiring rates, the level of separations and hiring is huge. When I was a professor, I would use the following analogy for my students. If you stand by a river, you can measure the water level. If you return the next day and measure again, you will likely find that the water level is unchanged-it is stable. But in fact, a massive amount of water has flowed downstream since the day before. The same goes for the labor market-there is a lot of churning even if the level of employment is stable.

The question is, does churn in the labor market matter? If so, is labor market churn bad or good? One could argue that this churn is inefficient. Why are people and firms wasting time swapping workers across jobs? If workers simply stayed at their firms, and firms never let them go, employment would be stable and resources would be saved from putting workers into new jobs. But would it mean the labor market is healthy?

The answer is that the churn in hiring and firing is actually good for the economy. This churn reflects a dynamic market that allows labor resources to be allocated to more productive uses. If a worker and firm are not in a good, productive match, then it is more efficient and better for the economy for the worker and firm to separate and look for new partners. When more productive matches are formed, productivity, real wages, and profits will be higher. In this situation, employment may not be stable, but it is healthier.

I believe this churn is what leads to the exceptional performance of the U.S. economy. The relative ease of starting businesses in the United States, compared with many other advanced economies, is a big advantage. The relative ease of firing employees, compared with many European Union economies, is surely not welcome by the workers affected, but cumulatively it was a factor that drove the stronger recovery in the United States from the pandemic recession. This flexibility in hiring and firing promotes a better match between skills of the worker and those demanded by businesses, making the most productive use of their abilities. As a result, this churn boosts the capacity of the economy and allows incomes to grow without inflationary pressure.

So, given this discussion, how do we interpret the current low hire, low fire economy? Does it indicate that the U.S. labor market has become less dynamic and less healthy, which has implications for the economic outlook and for monetary policy? I will first consider the possible causes of this lower dynamism and then the possible implications.

One explanation for the lower dynamism is that some of the decline in both hiring and firing may reflect, in part, a continuation of longer-run trends that were in place even before the pandemic. First, it is well known that the workforce is aging for a number of reasons: People are living longer and are healthier and more active at older ages; many members of the large post-World War II baby boom are in their 60s and 70s; and birth rates have declined, which increases the relative age of the workforce. This aging affects the dynamism of the labor market because older workers switch jobs less frequently, since many have managed over time to find better job matches and because older workers are less likely to relocate for work. The second trend is that the level of education of the workforce is increasing over time. More educated workers experience less job churn in general and, during downturns, face lower rates of job separations. Since 2010, the share of adults 25 and older with at least a bachelor's degree has increased from 28 percent to 37 percent.3

If these were the only reasons for the decline in labor market dynamism, then it would be at a level consistent with these trend factors, suggesting an appropriate degree of dynamism with no implications for monetary policy. But the data suggest that, even after accounting for these factors, labor market dynamism still seems somewhat low. There are several possible reasons.

One is that hiring and job-switching may have been restrained by the confluence of factors that have raised economic uncertainty since early 2025: the advent of AI, tariffs, changes in immigration policy and enforcement, and a general level of uncertainty about the economic outlook that has made business planning particularly challenging. One piece of evidence was a special question posed in the Federal Reserve's November 2025 Beige Book survey of economic conditions: Employers reported in November 2025 that hiring was unusually restrained because of uncertainty. I don't think uncertainty has diminished much since then. And another piece of evidence is in the most recent Beige Book, showing that several Fed Districts reported firms had delayed hiring or anticipate less job creation after investing in AI.

Another reason for low dynamism is that low firing may be a consequence of the huge surge in job-switching from 2020 to 2023 related to the pandemic. Workers in new jobs are less inclined to change jobs again, and that may be limiting job-switching. If this is a large factor, it may be temporary-workers are in their jobs for a median of three years before switching again, and we are nearing that threshold for the last of the pandemic job switchers. But it's possible they could be staying longer now if the job-switching triggered by the pandemic had been unusually effective at improving the matches between workers and jobs-many relocated or chased dreams and new careers and may not be as willing to switch again.

As you can tell, it is hard to pin down and properly weigh the possible causes of lower labor market dynamism and then judge how long that phenomenon might continue. This makes it hard to know the implications for the economic outlook and monetary policy.

But we can talk more constructively, I think, about the possible effects of the current low hire, low fire environment. While low layoffs imply that fewer workers experience unemployment, a low hiring rate means that those who do become unemployed may experience longer unemployment spells. And, in fact, the percentage of unemployed people who have been looking for work for more than six months has climbed steadily since 2022 and is now quite elevated for a period of economic expansion.4 Another logical consequence of lower dynamism in the labor market would be that new entrants, typically young and with less experience, are having a harder time finding jobs. I think anyone paying attention to the U.S. economy has been hearing about the challenges young workers are facing. Indeed, the share of new labor force entrants in unemployment has been rising and has reached close to the highest levels of the past twenty years.

Both these developments may reflect a labor market that is not as healthy as the headline unemployment rate indicates, with implications for the longer-term path of monetary policy. If hires and separations are low because worker matches have improved, then this may be a boost to productivity and can be largely ignored in assessing the state of the labor market. But I worry that today's labor market dynamism may be low due to impediments to mobility that are affecting long-term and youth unemployment, and this may lead to a less-efficient distribution of workers across jobs, hindering productivity growth. This possibility is important to monitor because productivity growth is a crucial factor in judging how fast the economy can grow without undesirable inflationary pressure. As I said earlier, I don't have the answers to the questions I have posed, but I believe the questions are worth asking and addressing with more research.

Let me put aside this discussion about the health of the labor market for now. What is important in the near term is that I see the labor market as stable and employment at a level close to the FOMC's maximum-employment goal.

By contrast, inflation is well above 2 percent and the focus of my attention. For reasons I explained at the start of this speech, I was willing to wait to tighten monetary policy at the FOMC's October meeting. Inconveniently for today's event, we will get consumer price index (CPI) inflation for October in a few hours. While I am hoping for an improvement over September, even if this occurs, I would still support a 25 basis point increase in the FOMC's policy rate at our December meeting. However, if inflation comes in substantially higher than I expect, more robust action by the FOMC may be called for.

Let's just say it. September's inflation data were bad. There was no silver lining. Inflation based on personal consumption expenditures (PCE), the measure targeted by the FOMC, rose at a monthly rate of 0.5 percent in September and 3.7 percent over the previous 12 months. Core PCE inflation, excluding food and energy prices, rose 0.3 percent in September and 3.1 percent from that time last year. Both these measures are too high, and I am particularly concerned about the breadth of price increases. Earlier this year, excessive inflation was driven by nonmarket prices that are estimated rather than observed by the government, and ones that I tend to discount as hard to measure and as an unreliable guide to the overall trend for core inflation. But now, two components with greater relevance to future inflation are elevated-core goods prices and those for core market-based services excluding housing. More than 70 percent of the components of core PCE service prices saw 12-month increases above 3 percent in September.

Later today, I will be looking to see whether this breadth of elevated inflation continues, including whether high-tech goods prices related to the AI buildout continue to rise at the very high rate of recent months. I also want to know if the run-up in energy prices of the past several months is being passed through to goods and services directly or indirectly, because of higher input costs. While I am pleased to see energy prices down from their high rates over the past week or so, they are still quite elevated relative to the start of the year, and the ultimate effect on inflation will depend on what levels are sustained.

Federal Reserve staff have been thinking hard about the effects on inflation of the AI buildout and elevated energy prices, and their findings do not encourage me to think that these factors will be fading anytime soon.

In one exercise, researchers tried to capture imminent price pressures with a textual analysis of the well-known surveys of purchasing managers conducted by the Institute for Supply Management (ISM).5 ISM surveys ask purchasing managers to list specific commodities, materials, and services whose prices rose or fell that month.6 Staff used these responses to construct monthly price pressure indexes that correspond with actual categories of the producer price index (PPI). They found these indexes provide information about future changes in producer prices and, as a result, should have some signal about future PCE inflation. For example, the index for high-tech products rose in December 2025 and jumped further in January 2026, ahead of an escalation in those goods prices that eventually showed up in the February PPI and inflation data. The most recent ISM data, for October, point to the possibility of more price increases ahead.

Some other Fed research indicates to me that energy price pressures may pass through to goods and services in a more sustained way than in the past.7 The researchers find a potential shift in the inflation process after the pandemic that suggests core inflation may be more responsive to energy shocks. Central bankers have tended to look through energy price shocks and expect that their effects on inflation will soon fade, but this new work cautions against taking too much comfort in this view. Their analysis suggests that, especially if oil prices were to remain elevated, these pressures could be larger than previously though and persist well into 2027.

And there are reasons to also expect elevated energy prices to persist. First, even as there is increased tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, that traffic is moving at great expense. The insurance now needed for ships making this passing, and the ship-to-ship transfer of oil necessary to guard against Iranian attacks, are reportedly boosting oil prices by $20 to $30 a barrel. A second problem is that diesel oil production is affected by limited refining capacity and other constraints. As a consequence, elevated prices for diesel in the United States are not expected to moderate as readily as crude oil prices would in a more peaceful Middle East.

To recap my economic outlook, economic activity is strong, the labor market is stable, but inflation is too high, well above the FOMC's 2 percent goal. This means that even if, as I expect, the monthly rate of inflation improves in October, I am leaning toward supporting an increase in our policy rate of 25 basis points at the FOMC's December meeting.

That's my plan if things proceed as I expect. But if the October CPI inflation data out later today are similar to the past two monthly readings-with core CPI inflation around 0.3 percent or even higher-then a stronger policy move may be needed. In that case, I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting. Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take.
1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Federal Reserve Board or the Federal Open Market Committee.

2. See Christopher J. Waller (2026), "The Signaling Value of the Summary of Economic Projections," speech delivered at the Istanbul Economic Forum, Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye, Istanbul, October 8.

3. Shakeena J. King and Daniela Mejía (2026), "Women Ages 65 and Over Now Make Up the Largest Share of Education Bachelor's Degree Holders," U.S. Census Bureau, America Counts: Stories Behind the Numbers, October 29.

4. The three-month moving average of workers reporting that they have been unemployed for 27 weeks or more increases from around 18 percent at the end of 2022 to more than 27 percent through September 2026.

5. Tomaz Cajner, Leland D. Crane, Christopher J. Kurz, Paul E. Soto, and Betsy Vrankovich (2026), "Pricing Sentiment: Measuring Input Cost Pressure from ISM Survey Responses," FEDS Notes (Washington: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, October 1).

6. For the prices paid question, respondents indicate whether prices increased, decreased, or stayed the same relative to the previous month and are asked to list specific commodities, materials, or services in an accompanying text field.

7. Andrea De Michelis, Musa Orak, Avani Pradhan, and Albert Queralto (2026), "The Effect of Oil Prices on Core Inflation: Recent Evidence from the Advanced Economies," FEDS Notes (Washington: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, November 9).

items.title: Bowman, Supervisory Modernization After Silicon Valley Bank
items.excerpt: Speech At the Bangkok Economic Festival, Reinventing Bretton Woods Committee, Bangkok, Thailand
body: Thank you for the invitation to join you today. It is good to be with you to discuss ensuring that the global financial system is positioned to adapt to the changing economic environment.1 The pace of change has been brisk. Our financial system is evolving rapidly. Therefore, it is important that we periodically review our regulatory and supervisory frameworks to consider how to best keep pace with that evolution.

Today, I will discuss three related aspects of supervisory modernization. First, I will describe some lessons learned from a newly released independent assessment of the failure of Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) about the importance of timely supervisory action. Second, I will discuss how the Federal Reserve is enhancing our supervisory effectiveness so that decisionmaking authority is clear and examiners are more accountable for taking timely action. And, third, I will describe how modernization can improve the work of supervision around the world, including under the direction of standard-setting bodies like the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) and the Financial Stability Board (FSB).

Independent Review of Silicon Valley Bank The failure of SVB in 2023 is a case study with critical lessons for bank supervisors at home and abroad. While prior reports on SVB provided important information, they were produced on an expedited basis with a limited scope and failed to comprehensively address important data related to the failure. As a result, these reports were incomplete and perpetuated a number of unreliable conclusions. That is why, earlier this year, I commissioned an independent review of the bank failure and the Federal Reserve's related supervision. The review closes prior gaps and corrects important misimpressions regarding SVB's failure. Its preliminary findings substantiate difficult but important critiques regarding Federal Reserve System supervision failures to act in a timely manner and to communicate actionable guidance to SVB.

A central finding is that supervisors had information about SVB's major vulnerabilities many months before its failure but did not make appropriate use of it. Frontline examiners, risk and surveillance specialists, and Reserve Bank and Board staff knew about SVB's exposure to interest rate and liquidity risk at least as early as nine full months before the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation took the bank into receivership. The review concludes that long-standing uncertainty about decisionmaking authority and the lack of clear accountability impeded timely decisionmaking.

The preliminary review also corrects earlier mischaracterization that social media was to blame for the run on SVB, and that the Fed's failure to act was caused by statutory tailoring or regulatory changes.2 Instead, the report notes long-standing problems in supervisory accountability and decisionmaking as the most significant contributors to the failure to issue timely critical enforcement actions related to core risks.

The Imperative of Timely Action While supervisory decisions must be grounded in evidence, legal authority, and judgment, the impact of supervisory decisions is only effective if delivered in time. When supervisors note vulnerabilities as they emerge, banks have more options and flexibility to course correct. At the point when weakness emerges, a bank can often gradually reduce exposure, strengthen its liquidity position, improve contingency planning, or raise capital under normal market conditions.

But where supervisors perpetually delay communication or action-to continually wait for additional evidence, more concurrence, or another committee meeting-supervision bogs down and loses effectiveness. Timely and efficient action is key to successful supervisory outcomes.

The review notes that supervisory attention at SVB often centered on process, procedure, governance, and controls rather than on mitigating the underlying interest rate and liquidity exposures. SVB had 54 matters requiring attention or immediate attention between 2019 and the time of its failure, yet none of those supervisory findings required the bank to address its core financial risks. In other words, a supervisory organization can be extremely busy and still fail to focus sufficiently on the risks that matter most. It can issue many findings, require firms to spend significant time and resources on remediation of less important process-related issues, and devote enormous resources to governance and process while failing to compel action on the vulnerabilities most capable of threatening the institution's existence.

Supervisory Prioritization and Accountability A supervisory culture of timely action must also be paired with clear roles and responsibilities so that supervisors are empowered to act. The independent review describes uncertainty within the Federal Reserve System about decision rights and lack of accountability across the supervisory system. In our structure, different groups identified risks, many others were expected to concur, and yet no individual clearly owned the obligation to reach a decision and propel action.

A modern supervisory organization needs clear answers to the basic questions of: who owns the decision to move forward? Who has authority to act? Who is accountable for ensuring that a material risk is addressed? And when different parts of the organization disagree, who is responsible to resolve that disagreement and keep pressing forward?

Modern supervisory organizations increasingly rely on surveillance, specialist teams, and data analysis that allow us to identify patterns across institutions. Those capabilities are enormously valuable. But identifying a risk matters only if there is a clear path from information to judgment and from judgment to action.
That is why we at the Federal Reserve System are considering ways to enhance our supervisory decisionmaking framework to ensure

In the fall of 2025, the Board published a Statement of Supervisory Operating Principles clearly stating our expectations about how supervisors should conduct supervision. We have refined those principles, most recently to incorporate lessons learned from the independent review of the 2023 banking stress. Publishing these principles further improves supervisory transparency and accountability. They refocus supervisory efforts on what matters most: early identification of material risks, exercising sound supervisory judgment, and a broad range of supervisory tools to enable timely and proportionate action to address material risks before they threaten the safety and soundness of an institution or the stability of the financial system.

International Implications and Proportionality The benefits of our supervisory modernization efforts are not limited to the Federal Reserve. They have implications far beyond the United States. Our reforms and the lessons learned from the independent review are equally applicable to supervisors around the world. As chair of the FSB's Standing Committee on Supervisory and Regulatory Cooperation, I have engaged many member jurisdictions to advance the FSB's regulatory and supervisory modernization agenda. The FSB's 2026 work program reflects that countries around the world are also evaluating whether regulatory and supervisory frameworks remain well suited for future financial systems.

There are important common themes in that work. Modernization is not about doing less. It is about more effectively prioritizing the things that matter the most. This includes concentrating on material risks, appropriately tailoring supervisory intensity, periodically reconsidering processes that may have accumulated over time to ensure they are still fit for purpose, and providing clarity so that supervisors can reach decisions quickly enough to make a difference.

Tailoring or proportionality does not mean weaker supervision. It means directing supervisory attention to the risks that are most material given the institution's size, complexity, activities, business model, interconnectedness, and potential impact on financial stability. A community bank engaged in conventional lending and deposit-taking does not require the same supervisory approach as a globally active institution engaged in complex trading and cross-border activities.

The purpose of prioritization is to distinguish issues that are genuinely capable of threatening safety and soundness from matters that may warrant attention but do not present the same degree of financial risk. This distinction requires supervisory judgment. And judgment inevitably requires making choices. A supervisory organization that treats every issue as equally important will tend to devote substantial attention to matters that are easiest to document, measure, and track, leaving other risks that require synthesis, experience, and enhanced judgment to receive less attention than they deserve. The objective should not be to maximize the number of findings that are issued. It should be to identify the risks that matter most and address them while there is still time to alter the trajectory.

International bodies, including the BCBS and the FSB, can help most in this supervisory modernization effort by focusing on their core mandates and by remaining evidence and data driven. They should prioritize work on areas that matter most-issues related to safety and soundness as well as financial stability.

International Lessons Learned The independent review of SVB shows that international standard-setting bodies, including the BCBS and the FSB, relied unquestioningly on incomplete reports compiled quickly and shortly after the failure of SVB. The independent review found that both the BCBS and the FSB took language nearly verbatim from other reports published in the United States that were not based on complete or accurate information. The independent review determined that these reports from the BCBS and the FSB generally repeated existing claims by other reports rather than independently verifying the information or increasing the breadth of evidence offered in their support.

As a result, the purported lessons learned put forth in the April 2023 report by then-Vice Chair Barr were initially used to justify additional regulatory work, including at the BCBS and the FSB. That work was inherently flawed because it was based on incomplete and faulty initial report findings, not a broader analysis like that provided by the independent review. Now, with the benefit of more comprehensive evidence and analysis, we can see that the international bodies' work based on prior results was not justified.

The BCBS's mandate is to strengthen regulation and supervision practices worldwide with the purpose of enhancing financial stability.3 Similarly, the FSB was established to coordinate and promote effective regulatory, supervisory, and other financial-sector policies in the interest of global financial stability.4 To maintain their credibility, these institutions must redouble their focus on material risks-those that affect safety and soundness or financial stability-while eschewing less valuable work that misdirects resources toward less valuable priorities.

These institutions must also seek to validate data and analysis that is relied upon for international standards and regulations. Simply accepting data and analysis without rigorous validation risks building international standards on flawed foundations, potentially undermining both the effectiveness of regulations and the credibility of these critical institutions.
Refocusing action on issues of material harm will allow these institutions to remain true to their core mandates and serve a more valuable purpose in fostering supervisory modernization.

Conclusion As we continue to modernize supervision and regulation at the Federal Reserve, and as we work with our international colleagues through the FSB and the BCBS on modernization, we must have the humility to continually reevaluate the effectiveness of our own supervisory processes. We should continue to assess how we make sure our supervisory efforts are keeping pace with a rapidly changing ecosystem. For instance, how do we organize our people to allocate authority and prioritize risks? How do we tailor supervisory intensity and equip our staff to quickly move from identifying a material vulnerability to taking appropriate action?

The financial system will continue to evolve rapidly. Our supervisory institutions must evolve with it. A critical measure of whether that modernization succeeds will be whether supervisors are able to identify the risks that matter and act decisively at the point when their actions can have the greatest impact.
Thank you.

items.title: Artrite o artrosi?
Waller, The Signaling Value of the Summary of Economic Projections
items.excerpt: Speech At the Istanbul Economic Forum, Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye, Istanbul, Türkiye
body: Thank you to the Central Bank of Türkiye for the opportunity to speak to you.1 I look forward today to hearing perspectives on the global economy and Türkiye's role in it, but I thought the most constructive use I can make of the valuable time you have granted me is to offer a brief update on the U.S. economy and then offer some thoughts on central bank communication.

As you know, in September the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) voted to raise our policy rate 25 basis points to 3.75 percent to 4 percent after nine months during which we held it steady. When monetary policy changes in this fashion, one question that most people ask is, what comes next? And I promise that I will do my best to answer that today, but first I will address another question raised by this shift in policy, which is, what changed? Was there new evidence, or did my thinking about the economy change? It turns out that the answer to this second question has a lot to do with the first one-about where policy goes from here.

I have mentioned that last month's increase in the federal funds rate came after nine months of holding it steady. When I ask "What changed?" I am obviously asking what changed in the seven weeks between July 29, when the FOMC voted to hold rates steady, and September 16, when we raised them. But I am also asking about what changed from the second half of 2025, when the FOMC reduced rates 75 basis points over three successive meetings. While it might seem to some that monetary policy has turned on a dime, or on one or two data points, in my case my decision last month was the culmination of factors that developed over the past year, and I would like to describe them.

When the FOMC cut rates from September through December 2025, we did so with inflation fairly close to our 2 percent target, after accounting for tariff effects that research found were passing through measures of inflation. At the same time, there was significant evidence of a weakening labor market, with an increase in unemployment over the first eight months of the year and very low job creation. Though the picture was less sharp after official data was interrupted because of the government shutdown that began on October 1, other data supported the view that the balance of risks to the FOMC's employment and inflation goals seemed clearly skewed toward employment. I considered our cuts to the policy rate last year as insurance against an economic slowdown.

But then, over the course of the first half of this year, the labor market appeared to stabilize, while progress on inflation stalled due in part to the conflict in the Middle East that drove energy prices very high. I supported no change in the policy rate in the spring and summer with the hope that the conflict would end soon and that the oil price surge would not have a lasting effect on inflation. And there were some signs of an easing of inflation. While headline inflation seesawed based on oil prices and the state of the Middle East conflict, core personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation-which excludes volatile food and energy prices-moderated to 0.1 percent in June and an initial estimate of 0.2 percent in July, later revised to 0.1 percent.

But other forces were undermining my faith in this progress. First, hopes for a quick ending to the Middle East conflict faded, and experts warned that low inventories and damaged infrastructure could keep oil prices high through 2027. Second, evidence mounted that the artificial intelligence buildout was significantly driving up high-tech consumer prices, and projections for the size of that buildout ballooned. Third, continuing trade conflicts threatened new tariffs that could put upward pressure on inflation yet again. In most cases, these were forces that became clearer as the year passed, swamping the fleeting signs of progress toward 2 percent inflation. When the first inflation reading for August came in hot just before the FOMC's September meeting, it was impossible to deny that inflation was still too high and not making sufficient progress toward our target.

While some suggested that monetary policy shifted in September based largely on the single data point of consumer price index inflation for August, I hope it is now apparent that this wasn't the case for me. Instead, it was a preponderance of evidence over several months that the risks for monetary policy had shifted, reflecting a strengthened labor market and a range of persistent inflationary forces. For me, this led to the judgment that the policy setting that the FOMC maintained from December 2025 through September of this year would not be sufficient to return inflation to 2 percent in a timely manner. My decision to change the stance of policy emerged over time because it is not one that I take lightly. With evidence that economic activity is strengthening in the second half of this year, I am not greatly concerned that tighter monetary policy threatens a damaging slowdown in the economy. But I am concerned that the recent acceleration in inflation-after what soon will be five and a half years of it above the FOMC's target-will lead consumers, investors, and price-setting businesses to revise up their expectations for future inflation.

Based on some key data released last week, I see the economy in roughly the same place as it was at the time of the FOMC's September meeting. While the number of jobs created was down overall, the employment report indicated that the labor market continued to be solid and stable in September. The unemployment rate remains relatively low and near the median of policymakers' projections of its longer-run level, while payroll gains are in the range of estimates of breakeven to keep the unemployment rate steady. August inflation data, which included revisions to the government's methodology, showed monthly core PCE inflation of 0.25 percent and the 12-month change at 3 percent. Looking at the history of 12-month core inflation, it has been between roughly 2.5 percent and 3.0 percent since the spring of 2024. This is obviously higher than we want, above our target, and not showing sufficient progress. Overall, the new data reinforce my view that the labor market is stable and inflation is too high. For at least the near term, policy will be focused on the inflation side of our mandate.

For the remainder of my remarks, I want to discuss a particular way of communicating the expected future stance of monetary policy that has the flavor of forward guidance but isn't forward guidance. Let me illustrate what I have in mind with an example.

Suppose that a majority of FOMC voters decide that policy needs to be more restrictive and that it is fairly clear to the public that some tightening is likely. What needs to be determined by both policymakers and markets is the number of rate hikes and the pace of rate hikes. Each policymaker thinks about his or her anticipated appropriate policy path to assist them in moving the economy toward the Fed's dual mandate. Markets estimate what the FOMC voters believe is the appropriate path of policy to assist them in pricing various assets.

So how could policymakers communicate the expected policy path to markets? There are several options. To explain, let's assume the number of hikes that policymakers have in mind is three 25 basis point hikes so that they anticipate policy will ultimately be 75 basis points higher than it currently is.

First, policymakers could choose to say nothing about the expected path of the policy rate. But that approach could surprise markets and create volatility. Without additional information, in an extreme case, they could price in zero or even potentially five hikes in future meetings. The point is that if too few or too many hikes are priced in, the change in financial conditions would mean too little or too much of an effect on economic activity.

Second, policymakers could use a strong form of forward guidance and communicate their support for raising the policy rate, let's say, every other meeting by 25 basis points until a total of 75 basis points worth of hikes has been enacted. The market would respond by pricing in 75 basis points of hikes over five meetings. While this eliminates any uncertainty about the future path of policy, it ignores the possibility that incoming data would suggest going faster or slower or hiking more or less than 75 basis points. Indeed, locking in a policy path over such a long period is unlikely to lead to good outcomes given the uncertainty around how the economy will evolve over time.

Finally, there is something in between these two approaches that I will call the signaling option. What I have in mind is that policymakers could signal that the policy rate will likely be hiked 75 basis points over some time interval-say, the next six months. However, policymakers do not say what the pace of hikes will be or how large of an increment the rate hike will be. And we could emphasize that the course of monetary policy is not predetermined and will depend on incoming data and its implications for our dual-mandate goals. This approach provides some information regarding what the terminal rate will be after hiking but allows the pace and the size of rate hikes to be data dependent. Simply put, policymakers could signal where they are likely headed while acknowledging that there is no fixed final destination-except for the achievement of price stability and maximum employment.

I see Federal Reserve policymakers' communications fitting in this last approach, both in their public remarks and their quarterly submissions of economic projections. The Summary of Economic Projections (SEP) is serving that signaling role for policymakers. The projections submitted at the September meeting showed that a large majority of FOMC participants believe it will be appropriate to raise rates at least once more this year. Sixteen of the 18 participants who submitted dots anticipated at least one more hike during the two remaining meetings this year. Four of those 16 expected two additional hikes. It gets a little complicated reading the dots for the full year of 2027, since they may reflect hikes early in the year and then cuts later in the year, but eight participants expect that rates will be 50 basis points higher at the end of 2027 than they are today.

Between the SEP and policymakers' outlook speeches that encompass their interpretation of additional economic data, markets have interpreted that the Committee is likely to raise the policy rate 50 basis points in the coming months. According to futures market prices for the federal funds rate as of yesterday, traders see an 85 percent chance of at least one hike by the end of the FOMC's December meeting and nearly 20 percent chance of two hikes. And, by the March 2027 meeting, markets see nearly an 80 percent chance of at least two hikes and a 33 percent chance of three or more hikes. This signaling helps to anchor the path of short-term interest rates but provides flexibility in adjusting rate hikes based on incoming data.

If the economic data continue to come in as expected, I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our 2 percent goal. But there is some flexibility about when those hikes will occur. The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time.
I think I will stop here to make sure there is enough time for our discussion.
1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Federal Reserve Board or the Federal Open Market Committee.
